summaryEn: Teaches you to give reasons: the weil clause and seit with the dative.
Teaches you to describe your career history in the past tense of written German.
Teaches you to describe yourself with a reservation: this may be so, but that is true.
Teaches you to say why you applied, using clauses of purpose.
Teaches you to ask for information politely with an indirect question.
Teaches you to describe flexible working with conditional clauses.
Teaches you to discuss pay in polite forms and shows the grammar of politeness.

titleEn: A rejection and a fresh try
summaryEn: Teaches you to order two past events: the earlier one finished, the later one built on it.
Teaches you to explain your decision to leave a job together with your reasons.
Teaches you to start a work conversation with a stranger and to ask questions politely.
Teaches you polite requests and wishes: Konjunktiv II with würde and könnten.
Teaches you to ask the right questions politely while viewing a flat.
Teaches you to read the language of a contract and shows how the passive is built.
Teaches you to raise a complaint without a row and drills the polite forms.
Teaches you to say what matters to you in a subordinate clause.
Teaches you to ask the landlord for a repair and to phrase the request formally.
Teaches you to dispute a service charge bill and shows the past form of the passive.
Teaches you how adjectives are declined in front of the noun.
Teaches you to organise jobs in time order: before, during and after.
Teaches you to discuss a temporary rental and drills stating a reservation again.
Teaches you to state a purpose with a damit clause when the two subjects differ.
Teaches you to state a purpose with the um … zu infinitive when the subject stays the same.
Teaches you to describe what runs against expectation, with an obwohl clause and the adverb trotzdem.
Teaches you to use als for a single event in the past and wenn for repeated events and the future.
Teaches you to say what happened first, with nachdem and the past perfect.
Teaches you to link events with bevor (before) and während (while).
Teaches you to state a result, or an unexpected one, with main-clause adverbs and verb-second order.
Teaches you to say that two things rise together, with je … desto.
Teaches you to offer alternatives, to say both and to say neither, with paired conjunctions.
Teaches you to combine the module's connectors in one story: zuerst, nachdem, während, deshalb, am Ende.
Teaches you to define a person by what they do: der, die, das.
Teaches you that der becomes den when the thing defined is the object of the clause.
Teaches you that the relative pronoun is dem, der or denen after verbs that take the dative.
Teaches you that when a preposition comes first, it is the preposition that sets the case.
Teaches you to describe what you dream of, with relative clauses that take their preposition from the verb.
Teaches you to build relative clauses with jemand, niemand and plural nouns.
Teaches you to describe an object whose name you do not know, and to use was after alles and etwas.
Teaches you the difference between an dem, in dem and wo when you describe a place.
Teaches you to describe a lost item to an official, using relative clauses.
Teaches you to recommend a dish and its ingredients with relative clauses.
Teaches you to build a passive sentence with werden when who does it does not matter.
Teaches you to build the past passive with wurde and to tell the form worden apart.
Teaches you to understand the formal passive of residence procedures and to ask about them.
Teaches you to appeal against an official decision in writing and to phrase the request with dass.
Teaches you to describe an official process in order, with passive and conditional clauses.
Teaches you to use the passive and the active each in its place while describing a tax return.
Teaches you to report damage in order and to say what happened first with the past perfect.
Teaches you the most polite request patterns for postponing an official appointment.
Teaches you the language of the document that authorises someone to act on your behalf.
Teaches you to ask about official details you do not know, with indirect question patterns.
